{"id": "c66bd674-40f8-4f6b-b056-fed834e3926a", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_HgipfLwjIpAlmSM8FdtyTb", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"How does throttling on my global secondary index affect my Amazon DynamoDB table?\",\"context\":\"Short description\\n-----------------\\n\\nThrottling on a GSI affects the base table in different ways. The effect depends on whether the throttling is for read activity or for write activity:\\n\\n* When a GSI has insufficient read capacity, throttling doesn't affect the base table.\\n* When a GSI has insufficient write capacity, throttling results in write operations that fail on the base table or any of its GSIs.\\n\\nFor more information, see [Using global secondary indexes in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GSI.html).\\n\\nResolution\\n----------\\n\\nTo prevent throttling, follow these steps:\\n\\n* Be sure that the provisioned write capacity for each GSI is equal to or greater than the provisioned write capacity of the base table. To modify the provisioned throughput of a GSI, use the [UpdateTable](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_UpdateTable.html) operation. If you turned on automatic scaling for the base table, then it's a best practice to apply the same settings to the GSI. To do this, choose **Copy from base table** in the DynamoDB console. For best performance, turn on **Use the same read/write capacity settings for all global secondary indexes**. This allows DynamoDB auto scaling to uniformly scale all the global secondary indexes on the base table. For more information, see [Activating DynamoDB auto scaling on existing tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/AutoScaling.Console.html#AutoScaling.Console.ExistingTable).\\n* Be sure that the GSI's partition key distributes read and write operations as evenly as possible across partitions. This helps prevent hot partitions and therefore throttling. For more information, see [Designing partition keys to distribute your workload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-uniform-load.html).\\n* To identify the most frequently throttled keys, use [Amazon CloudWatch Contributor Insights for DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/contributorinsights.html)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/dynamodb-gsi-throttling-table\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Why is my on-demand DynamoDB table throttling?\",\"context\":\"### The GSI of your table experiences throttling\\n\\nIf your DynamoDB table has a global secondary index (GSI) that's throttling, then the throttling might create back-pressure throttling on the base table. For more information, see [Understanding GSI write throttling and back pressure in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/gsi-throttling.html) and [Using GSIs in DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GSI.html)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/on-demand-table-throttling-dynamodb\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Understanding Global Secondary Index (GSI) write throttling and back pressure in DynamoDB\",\"context\":\"## Types of GSI throttling\\n\\nGSI back-pressure throttling manifests through different exception types depending\\non the specific capacity constraint:\\n\\n* **GSI provisioned capacity exceeded:** Occurs\\n when the GSI lacks sufficient write capacity units to handle updates from\\n base table operations. This produces a\\n `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException` with the reason\\n IndexWriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded, and\\n the `ResourceArn` points directly to the specific GSI\\n experiencing capacity constraints.\\n* **GSI on-demand maximum throughput\\n exceeded:** Occurs when GSI write operations surpass configured\\n maximum limits on on-demand tables. This produces a\\n `ThrottlingException` with the reason IndexWriteMaxOnDemandThroughputExceeded,\\n identifying the specific GSI with configured throughput restrictions.\\n* **GSI partition limits exceeded:** Happens\\n when individual GSI partitions exceed their throughput limits (hot\\n partitions), even if overall GSI capacity appears sufficient. This generates\\n a `ThrottlingException` with the reason IndexWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded,\\n indicating hot partition issues on the specific GSI identified in the\\n `ResourceArn`. This is particularly important because GSI\\n partition distribution may differ significantly from the base table's\\n partition distribution, creating hot spots in the GSI even when base table\\n access is evenly distributed.\\n* **GSI account limits exceeded:** Triggers\\n when write operations to a specific GSI exceed the per-table (or any\\n individual GSI within that table) regional throughput boundaries set at the\\n account level. DynamoDB returns a `ThrottlingException` with the\\n reason IndexWriteAccountLimitExceeded, pointing to the\\n GSI that pushed its usage beyond account limits. This throttling occurs\\n independently for each GSI that surpasses the limit. For information about\\n per-table, per-account,regional, service quotas, see Quotas in Amazon DynamoDB\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/gsi-throttling.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify DynamoDB GSI throttling propagates to base table writes"}

{"id": "eb014d29-b9b5-47ab-86ec-728a95aebb88", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This confirms the mechanism — this is classic **GSI back-pressure throttling**, and it fully explains your symptom pattern.

**Why base-table writes get throttled/slowed when the base table shows zero `WriteThrottleEvents`:**

Every `PutItem` against `orders-prod` has to propagate the same write to `orders-by-status` synchronously as part of the write path. If the GSI doesn't have enough write capacity to absorb that propagation, DynamoDB throttles the *base table operation itself* — it doesn't throttle the GSI update separately. The result:

- The GSI's own `WriteThrottleEvents` metric lights up (your 9 periods, 14:05–14:20).
- The base table's `WriteThrottleEvents` metric stays at zero — the base table was never short on its own provisioned capacity, so from the table's perspective nothing was throttled.
- But `PutItem` requests that need to update that GSI get rejected/retried via back-pressure, which shows up as `ThrottledRequests` for the `PutItem` operation and as elevated `PutItem` p99 latency (retries + backoff inflate the client-observed latency) — exactly your 140 ms vs 20 ms baseline in 8 of 9 periods.

So the causal chain is: **GSI `orders-by-status` under-provisioned for writes → GSI write capacity exceeded → back-pressure throttling applied to base-table `PutItem` → elevated `PutItem` p99 + `ThrottledRequests`, with base-table `WriteThrottleEvents` untouched.**

This matches the provisioned-capacity variant specifically: since the table is provisioned (not on-demand), the likely cause is `IndexWriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded` — the GSI's provisioned WCUs are lower than what the base table's write volume demands, or the GSI has a hot partition key (e.g., `status` has low cardinality — few distinct status values concentrate writes on very few GSI partitions, exceeding per-partition throughput even if aggregate GSI capacity looks fine).

**To confirm which:**
- Compare GSI provisioned WCU vs. base table provisioned WCU — if GSI WCU < base table WCU, that's the straightforward fix (raise GSI write capacity to match or exceed the base table, or match auto-scaling settings).
- If GSI WCU looks adequate in aggregate, check Contributor Insights for `orders-by-status` to see if a small number of `status` key values are absorbing most writes (hot partition) — that needs a key redesign (e.g., add a sharding suffix to spread status values), not just a capacity bump.

Want me to look at the actual provisioned WCU settings and Contributor Insights data for `orders-by-status` to narrow this down further?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
